I was going to make this comment on your RFK video. But instead I am going to leave it here so you hopefully see it:

As a future medicine student who wants to be specialized in family medicine and whose mother is also a doctor specialized in family medicine, you are a role model to the future doctor I want to become. You remind me a lot about my mother. You have similar personalities and also share the same opinions with the same mindset of being by the patients side. You are incredibly inspiring and I love the way you talk to the non-specialized public (like in the jubilee podcast) to make them understand that you are not on RFK, Trump---science's or any politician's side. You are on the patients side. Always. And you want them to make the decision that will leave them more at peace with themselves. Sometimes, you already know the right answer. Sometimes you just ask the patient. But you are always on their side. 

You are a huge inspiration to me and I hope when I do become a doctor, I am half as good as you and my mother as a family medicine-specialized doctor.

Thanks for being a good role model and for also saving my life. We also are always by your side.

comments.text:
I appreciate the video and the information compiled and shared, but i think its a disservice to leave out information about the people we lost to suicide, even 'accidental', or at the very least who had lifelong severe mental health struggles. Heath Ledger struggled with severe depression and insomnia, leading to his mixing of meds to attempt to sleep, Robbin Williams struggled with anxiety and depression and substance abuse far before LBD came along, Carrie Fisher famously struggled with bipolar II. 

Talking about their deaths and substance abuse without talking about their severe mental health struggles leaves nuance at the door and only further stigmatisez both of these struggles. They are people who were failed by the stigmas of their suffering and were either too uninformed or too afraid to seek professional psychological and psychiatric help, and even those who did so got too little of it, too late. This is information and nuance that should NOT be missing from their stories, especially when there is money being made and there are no sources anywhere for people to learn more.
comments.author: @andreeadoca1550

comments.text:
Have you done one of these on somewhat smaller, but nonetheless impactful, creatives? I got a couple good ones to start you off:

- First, a big one: Akira Toriyama, one of the greatest mangaka (manga creators) of all time, perhaps best known as the visionary behind one of the biggest franchises ever, "Dragon Ball". On Mar 1, 2024, at the age of 68, he died of an acute subdural hematoma, a type of bleeding in the brain - his production company announced his passing a week later, to an outpouring of tributes from fans, former collaborators, fellow manga creators inspired by his long list of works, and even a few governments (not just Japan).

- Speaking of manga: Kazuo Takahashi, aka Kazuki Takahashi, best known as the creator of "Yu-Gi-Oh!" for the publication Weekly Shōnen Jump (same as "Dragon Ball", btw) which originally ran from 1996-2004; it spawned an anime, multiple sequel/spin-off series, and the best-selling trading card game of all time (according to Guinness World Records). On July 6, 2022, his lifeless body was found about 300 m (960 ft) off the shore of Nago, Okinawa, by the Japanese Coast Guard; cause of death was listed as drowning. Later reports say Takahashi died on the 4th, while assisting in the rescue of three others caught in a rip current - he died saving lives.


- Finally, a smaller, but still very influential to indie animation: Monty Oum, an indie animator who'd probably be best known for his work at Rooster Teeth, including creating their best series "RWBY" [pronounced "ruby"]. During a "simple medical procedure" on Jan 22, 2015, between production of RWBY seasons 2 and 3, he had an unspecified severe allergic reaction and fell into a coma for 10 days - I remember hearing it was to some kind of medicine, like maybe penicillin? (but also, this was over 10 years ago, so don't quote me on anything) - before he died from anaphylaxis on Feb 1, at only 33 years old.

If anyone else has a suggestion, please, share it with the class!

Another thing to know about Paul Newman:  He founded the "Hole in the Wall Gang Camp"--named after the group in "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid"--which provides a "summer camp" experience to kids with cancer.  I went to uni with someone who had been a councilor at the camp, and he said that all the councilors were cancer survivors.  This did three things:  1) they understood everything that the kids were going through, and (most importantly, according to my friend) 2) the kids couldn't pull the "I have cancer!" card to manipulate the councilors. John said that a lot of the kids would try that in the first couple days, and he'd recount his battle with leukemia, ask them questions about their treatments, and let them know that they were among like people and didn't need to play those games, and finally 3) show the kids strong (young) adults who not only survived, but thrived.

I’ve lived with epilepsy all my life and I can tell you, it’s not easy. Having to be careful about what you do, regulate your stress, worry about how far you can walk, what volume you can listen to your music on, which roller coasters you can ride. And it can be very dangerous and not just because of SUDEP.

I believe I read somewhere that your skull softens when you have a seizure to prevent you from doing as much damage to the brain when you fall. But that also makes the skull easier to break and I almost did when I had a seizure outside and almost hit it on a river rock as I went down. And if you don’t do that, the pain itself is immense. People often ask me what it feels like and the only way I can describe it is it feels like I’m getting electrocuted from the inside out.

transcript: Every year at the Oscars, we see a heartfelt inmemoriam segment honoring the movie stars who have passed away, but we don't always get to hear about how they died. And sometimes it's unbelievable. I'm talking mysterious drownings, car accidents, and one mass murdering cult leader. So, so tragic. But let's start with Chadwick Boseman, known to many as Black Panther, one of the defining stars of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. In 2016, right on the heels of debuting his role as King Tchala in Captain America: Civil War, Chadwick was diagnosed with stage three colon cancer. He kept the diagnosis a secret from almost everyone. Only a few non-family members knew. And despite this diagnosis, he continued working, privately, receiving chemotherapy treatments and surgeries to fight the illness in between shooting days. It wasn't enough, taking his life in 2020 at just 43 years old. He wasn't the first young star of a superhero franchise to pass though, joining the ranks of Heath Ledger, who famously played the Joker in Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight. At the age of just 26 in his Manhattan apartment, the Australian actor died from acute intoxication by the combined effects of oxycodone, hydrocodone, dasipam, tamasazipam, alprazilam and doxial amine, sleep medications, anxiety medications, and painkillers. Perhaps the doses of the medications weren't that high, but it was really this very unusual cocktail of medications that all have a side effect of respiratory depression. He likely fell asleep, suppressed his respiratory drive, and never woke up. Robin Williams was one of the most adored movie stars of all time. No doubt appearing in Something You've Loved, whether it be The Genie in Aladdin or one of my all-time favorites, Goodwill Hunting. In his final years of life, Robin began developing unusual symptoms, including tremors. He thought it was Parkinson's, a degenerative disease that causes the nervous system to worsen over time. An autopsy later showed Robin did not have Parkinson's. He actually suffered from a rare incurable disease called Louisbody dementia or LBD. These abnormal protein deposits called Louis bodies infiltrated his brain and accelerated his paranoia, anxiety, and depression. Because he hadn't been properly diagnosed, doctors sometimes prescribed him anti-anxiety medications that could paradoxically make his paranoia worse. Experts later told Robin's wife, Susan, that in retrospect, he showed 39 of the 40 common symptoms of LBD, with the only outstanding one being hallucinations. Susan believes Robin probably was experiencing hallucinations but kept them to himself. Eventually, the mental nightmare Robin was facing became too much and he died at the age of 63. Shan Connory had one of the most legendary accents in Hollywood, which helped propel him to international stardom as agent 0007 James Bond. He lived until the age of 90 when he died in his sleep at his home in the Bahamas from heart failure related to atrial fibrillation and respiratory failure due to pneumonia and infection of the lungs. He may have been the first James Bond, but he was technically the second Bond we lost behind Roger Moore. He never got the same credit as Shan Connory did for originating the role, but he did match him for playing 007 times in the 1970s and 80s. He died in Switzerland after a short battle with cancer. Carrie Fischer was an actress who originated the role of Princess Leia in Star Wars. In 2016, she fell asleep on a long flight and struggled to wake up as they neared landing. She eventually started vomiting and was rushed to a hospital where she died several days later. According to the coroner's statement, the 60-year-old actress's cause of death was listed as cardiac arrest related to sleep apnea with other factors like atherosclerotic, heart disease, and drug use. Her toxicology report found traces of cocaine, methadone, MDMA, alcohol, and opiates in her system. While she famously played an intergalactic princess, she was a member of Hollywood royalty as well. She was the daughter of Debbie Reynolds, the singer and actress who performed on screen and on stage for nearly 70 years. She lived to the age of 84 before dying from a stroke one day after Carrie passed. Debbie's son said that the shock and trauma of Carrie's passing was so intense that it triggered the stroke, saying she's gone to be with Carrie. Debbie's breakout performance came at just 19 years old when she starred in Singing in the Rain. But she's not the youngest breakout star on our list. That goes to Shirley Temple, one of the very first child stars, who some credit with saving the American spirit from the depths of the Great Depression. That's not revisionist history either. President FDR was quoted as saying, "As long as our country has Shirley Temple, we'll be all right." By the age of 6 years old, she was making $1,250 a week or around $30,000 today. She appeared in 46 feature films by the time she was just 13 and retired from acting around 1950. She transitioned into politics serving as the US delegate to the United Nations and later served as the US ambassador to Ghana and Czechoslovakia. In 1972, she received a mastctomy, a procedure to surgically remove breast tissue after they found the lump. Her public confidence in getting the procedure helped reduce its stigma and may have saved the lives of countless women to this day. According to her death certificate, she died at 85 years old of pneumonia and COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. During her rapid ascent as an actress, she was considered for the historic part of Dorothy in the Wizard of Oz, but it ultimately went to Judy Garland. She was perhaps the most talented performer on this list, a brilliant singer, dancer, and actor, but was doomed from an early age by a predatory Hollywood studio system. Her talent was spotted immediately, and she was put to work as a child. To regulate her performances, her studio handlers made her an addict, giving her sleeping pills at night and other drugs to keep her awake for long hours on set. She was just a kid when the addiction began and tragically she was never able to escape it. At the age of 47, she was found dead in her bathroom by her husband, slumped over her toilet after an overdose of barbituates, a type of insomnia medication we no longer use for that purpose. James Dean was the coolest guy in Hollywood. By his early 20s, he had already established himself as the young, handsome, heartthrob destined for showbiz stardom. Unfortunately, those dreams were cut short when one evening the 24 year old leading man was involved in a car accident in central California on his way to a race in Selenus. Another driver collided with James headon and left him with massive internal injuries. Broken arms, legs, a broken neck. An ambulance rushed to the scene and raced James to a hospital where he was pronounced dead on arrival. The driver of the other car only sustained minor injuries. Not long after his passing, his film Rebel Without a Cause was released in theaters, which he starred in alongside Natalie Wood, whose death is still debated to this day. In 1981, Natalie, her husband, Robert Wagner, Christopher Walkin, and a boat captain were all aboard the Splendor near Catalina Island off the coast of Los Angeles. According to multiple witnesses and reports, there was some sort of argument on the boat late in the evening. Not long after, the boat's dinghy disappeared along with Natalie. The authorities were called and a search continued into the night. Just before the break of dawn, the dinghy was found in an isolated cove with Natalie's lifeless body floating nearby. The initial cause of death was ruled accidental drowning with many believing Natalie took the dinghy to get away from the argument happening on the splendor, then somehow fell overboard and was unable to pull herself to safety. Others believe her husband, Robert, may have been to blame and potentially murdered his own wife. Nothing has ever been proven, but the case was reopened in 2011, and the cause of death was changed to drowning and other undetermined factors, stating how wood ended up in the water is not clearly established, so we may never know. Gene Hackman won two Oscars, one for the French Connection, which basically invented the modern car chase, and the other for best picture winner Unforgiven, starring Clint Eastwood. His long and storied career makes his passing that much more unsettling. In 2025, both Gan and his wife Betsy were found dead in their New Mexico home with no explanation. After careful investigation, it's believed that Betsy died of haunt virus pulmonary syndrome. It's a rodentborn disease that can lead to severe flu-l like symptoms. Gene is believed to have died several days later from heart disease. But if Betsy was ill and eventually died, why wouldn't Jean have called 911? We may never know for sure, but experts speculate Gene was in the advanced stages of Alzheimer's disease, a progressive brain disorder that destroys memories and your ability to perform even the most basic functions. His brain possibly deteriorated to the point where he may not even realize Betsy was dead and he was unable to take care of himself. Bruce Lee is the most influential martial artist in history, having largely introduced it into Western culture through his films like Enter the Dragon and Fists of Fury. He was a deeply spiritual and philosophical thinker, popularizing the quote, >> I said, empty your mind, be formless, shapeless like water. Be water, my friend. >> Ironically, water may have been one of the factors that killed him. It hasn't been fully confirmed exactly how Bruce Lee died at the age of 32 in Hong Kong, with some blaming a violent Chinese gang murder. His official cause of death was stated as cerebral edema caused by misadventure with hypersensitivity to equacase, a drug that combines aspirin and merobamate. During his autopsy, it was discovered that his brain was carrying excess water. But why? Experts have speculated it could have been due to the stroke he suffered from repeated head trauma as a martial artist. Others argued that it was due to heat stroke caused by unusually high temperatures in Hong Kong and the fact that Bruce had some of his underarm sweat glands removed just one month before his death, believing that sweat was not photogenic on the big screen. Interestingly, some researchers recently looked into the case and made a strong argument for hyponetriia being the cause. That's low sodium in the blood. Regardless, the next time you see some awesome kung fu in a movie, you could thank Bruce Lee for bringing that to us. Philip Seymour Hoffman was one of the most talented actors of his generation, winning an Oscar in 2006 for his portrayal of the writer Truman Capot and stealing scenes in virtually every film and franchise he starred in. Despite his prolific persona on screen, friends and peers have said he faced a lifelong battle with addiction. In 2014, he failed to pick up his children, and a friend went to his New York apartment to make sure he was okay. What his friend found was devastating. An apartment riddled with envelopes of heroin and prescription drug bottles. Philip Seymour Hoffman was found dead in his bathtub with a needle sticking out of his arm. The medical examiner said he died of accidental acute mixed drug intoxication, including heroin, cocaine, benzoazipines, and amphetamine. As a physician, the opioid crisis is one I see up close.
